title: Reflexive, Symmetric, Antisymmetric and Asymmetric Relations
quickIdea: Read the four properties off the 0/1 matrix: reflexive is a full diagonal, symmetric is a mirror-symmetric matrix, antisymmetric forbids both cells of a mirror pair, asymmetric also forbids the diagonal.
remember: A relation R on A is reflexive when (a, a) is in R for every a in A; it is irreflexive when (a, a) is in R for no a.
R is symmetric when (a, b) in R implies (b, a) in R, and antisymmetric when (a, b) and (b, a) both in R forces a = b.
Asymmetric means (a, b) in R implies (b, a) not in R; on a set this is exactly irreflexive plus antisymmetric.
Antisymmetric is not the negation of symmetric. The identity relation is both symmetric and antisymmetric, and a relation can be neither.
Symmetric and antisymmetric together force R to be a subset of the identity relation, so there are 2 to the n such relations on an n-element set.

On an n-element set: all relations 2 to the (n squared); reflexive and irreflexive 2 to the (n squared minus n); symmetric 2 to the n(n+1)/2; antisymmetric 2 to the n times 3 to the n(n-1)/2; asymmetric 3 to the n(n-1)/2; reflexive and symmetric 2 to the n(n-1)/2.
Neither reflexive nor irreflexive is 2 to the (n squared) minus 2 times 2 to the (n squared minus n), because the reflexive and irreflexive relations are disjoint.
The matrix picture is the fastest route in the exam: the diagonal has n cells, the cells off the diagonal form n(n-1)/2 mirror pairs.
For a relation between different sets A and B only symmetry-type questions make sense with care; reflexivity needs a relation from A to A.

example.prompt: A = {1, 2, 3} and R = {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (1,2), (2,1)}. Decide reflexivity, symmetry, antisymmetry and transitivity.
example.work: All three diagonal pairs are present, so R is reflexive. (1,2) is accompanied by (2,1), and no other off-diagonal pair exists, so R is symmetric. Because (1,2) and (2,1) are both present with 1 not equal to 2, R is not antisymmetric. For transitivity, (1,2) and (2,1) force (1,1), which is present, and (2,1) and (1,2) force (2,2), which is present, so R is transitive.
example.answer: R is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, not antisymmetric: it is the equivalence relation whose classes are {1, 2} and {3}.

gateAngle: GATE CS 2015 Set 3 Q.41 defines a relation on ordered pairs by p - s = q - r and asks which pair of properties holds; the answer is that it is symmetric but not reflexive, and the reflexivity check is the whole question.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: See GATE CS 2015 Set 3 Q.41 in the linked PYQs: R on ordered pairs of positive integers with (p,q) R (r,s) when p - s = q - r.
variations.why: Reflexivity would need p - q = q - p, that is p = q, which fails for (1,2). Symmetry follows because p - s = q - r is the same equation as r - q = s - p.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: On A = {1, 2, 3}, how many relations are symmetric and antisymmetric, and how many are antisymmetric in total?
variations.why: Symmetric and antisymmetric relations are the subsets of the identity relation, so 2 cubed = 8. Antisymmetric relations are 2 cubed times 3 cubed = 8 times 27 = 216, because each of the three mirror pairs has three allowed states.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: On a 4-element set, how many relations are reflexive and symmetric but not antisymmetric?
variations.why: Reflexive and symmetric relations number 2 to the n(n-1)/2 = 2 to the 6 = 64; exactly one of them, the identity, is also antisymmetric, so 63 remain.

trap.what: Treating antisymmetric as 'not symmetric', or forgetting that a relation may be neither reflexive nor irreflexive.
trap.why: The two properties constrain different things: symmetry forbids one-sided pairs being absent, antisymmetry forbids two-sided pairs between distinct elements. A relation can satisfy both (identity), neither (a single off-diagonal pair with no diagonal), or one only.
trap.counterexample: On A = {1, 2} take R = {(1,1), (1,2)}. It has one diagonal pair but not the other, so it is neither reflexive nor irreflexive; it is antisymmetric and transitive, and not symmetric. On the same set R' = {(1,2)} is irreflexive, antisymmetric and transitive, so a single off-diagonal pair satisfies three of the four properties at once.

check.question: On a 3-element set, how many relations are symmetric and how many are reflexive?
check.explanation: Symmetric relations are 2 to the n(n+1)/2 = 2 to the 6 = 64, choosing freely on the diagonal and on each of the three mirror pairs. Reflexive relations are 2 to the n(n-1) = 2 to the 6 = 64, with the diagonal forced and the six off-diagonal cells free. The equality of the two numbers here is a coincidence of n = 3.
